config.description: Nikhilam-style arrow matrix for 103×104: each factor with its surplus (+3, +4) in its own row; diagonal crosswise arrows give the left lane 100+3+4 = 107, the deviation column multiplies down to the right lane 12; concatenate to 10712.
config.textual_equivalent: 103×104 by Yavadunam/Nikhilam: base 100, surpluses +3 and +4. Left part = 100 + 3 + 4 = 107. Right part = 3×4 = 12. Concatenate 107|12 = 10712.

solution.description: Both factors, 103 and 104, sit just above 100, so 100 is the nearest power of ten to measure from. Every deviation in this problem is taken against that base.

solution.operation: Find the surpluss from the base
solution.description: Measure each factor against the base: 103 is 3 above 100 and 104 is 4 above, so the deviations are plus 3 and plus 4. Both signs are positive because both factors lie above the base.

solution.operation: Apply the Yavadunam Sutra formula for multiplication
solution.description: State the rule before applying it: the two deviations are cross-added onto the base to build the left part of the answer, and multiplied together to build the right part. The next two steps carry out those two halves separately.

solution.operation: Compute the left part by cross-operation
solution.description: Cross-add the deviations onto the base: 100 plus 3 plus 4 gives 107. Taking 103 and adding the other factor's deviation of 4, or 104 plus 3, gives the same 107, which is why this is called a cross-operation.
Multiply the two deviations with each other: 3 times 4 gives 12. That product is the right part of the answer, and it has to fit the slot whose width is set by the two zeros in the base 100.

solution.operation: Pad the right part to 2 digit(s)
solution.description: Check the width of the right part. The base 100 has two zeros, so the right slot holds exactly two digits. 12 already has two digits, so it needs no leading zero and stands as it is.

Set the two parts side by side, left part first: 107 followed by the two-digit block 12 reads as 10712. No carry into the left part is needed, because the right part did not overflow its two-digit slot.
Check the shortcut against ordinary long multiplication: 103 times 104 really does give 10712, so the base method and the standard method agree.

common_mistakes: Adding the two deviations only to each other and writing 3 plus 4 equals 7 as the left part, instead of adding both onto the base to get 100 plus 3 plus 4 equals 107.
Building the right part from a whole factor rather than from the deviations, for example 103 times 4, instead of multiplying the deviations 3 times 4 to get 12.

config.description: Place-value slot assembly for 98×102 = 9996: cross-operation gives left slot 100 and deviation product −4 is negative, so borrow 1 hundred from the left slot (100 → 99) and add it to the right slot (−4 + 100 = 96).
config.textual_equivalent: 98×102 by Yavadunam/Nikhilam: base 100, deviations −2 and +2. Left = 100 − 2 + 2 = 100; right = (−2)×(+2) = −4 is negative, so borrow 1 from the left: left 99, right 100 − 4 = 96. Answer 99|96 = 9996.

solution.description: 98 and 102 both lie within a few units of 100, so 100 is the nearest power of ten to work from and becomes the base for both deviations.

solution.operation: Find the deficiency/surpluss from the base
solution.description: Measure each factor against the base: 98 falls 2 short of 100 while 102 runs 2 past it, so the deviations are minus 2 and plus 2. Hold on to those signs; they control both the cross-addition and the sign of the right part.

solution.operation: Apply the Yavadunam Sutra formula for multiplication
solution.description: State the rule before applying it: cross-add the deviations onto the base for the left part, and multiply the deviations together for the right part. The steps that follow work each half in turn.

solution.operation: Compute the left part by cross-operation
solution.description: Cross-add onto the base: 100 minus 2 plus 2 comes back to exactly 100. Here one factor is below the base by as much as the other is above it, so the deviations cancel and the left part is the base itself.

Multiply the deviations: minus 2 times plus 2 gives minus 4. One factor sat below the base and the other above, so the right part comes out negative and cannot be written into the two-digit slot as it stands.

solution.operation: Adjust for negative right part (borrow from left)
solution.result: \text{Right part is negative: } -4 \\ \text{Borrow 1 from left: } 100 - 1 = 99 \\ \text{Adjusted right: } 100 + (-4) = 96
solution.description: Repair the negative right part by borrowing one hundred from the left part. The left part drops from 100 to 99, and that borrowed hundred is handed to the right part, turning minus 4 into 100 minus 4 equals 96. Nothing is lost; value has only moved between the two slots.
Set the adjusted parts side by side: left part 99 followed by the two-digit block 96 reads as 9996.
Check the shortcut against ordinary long multiplication: 98 times 102 really does give 9996, confirming that the borrow was handled correctly.

common_mistakes: Writing the negative deviation product straight into the answer as 100 and minus 4, giving 1004 or 100-4, instead of borrowing to reach 99 and 96.
Borrowing the hundred from the left part but forgetting to add it to the right, ending up with 99 and 4 as 9904 rather than 9996.
Dropping the plus sign when cross-adding and computing 100 minus 2 minus 2 equals 96, instead of 100 minus 2 plus 2 equals 100.

solution.operation: Adjust for negative right part (borrow from left)
solution.result: \text{Right part is negative: } -25 \\ \text{Borrow 1 from left: } 100 - 1 = 99 \\ \text{Adjusted right: } 100 + (-25) = 75
solution.description: Repair the negative right part by borrowing one hundred from the left part. The left part falls from 100 to 99, and the borrowed hundred absorbs the shortfall on the right: 100 minus 25 equals 75. The total value is unchanged.

Borrowing 1 from the left part but subtracting 25 from nothing, writing 99 and 25 as 9925 rather than adding the borrowed hundred first to get 75.

solution.description: 996 lies close to 1000, so 1000 is the nearest power of ten to square against. Its three zeros will also set the width of the right part later on.

solution.operation: Find the deficiency from the base
solution.description: Measure 996 against the base: it falls 4 short of 1000, so the deficiency is minus 4. The negative sign records that the number is below the base.

State the Yavadunam rule for squaring before applying it: lessen the number by its own deficiency to build the left part, which amounts to adding twice the deficiency to the base, and set down the square of the deficiency as the right part.
Build the left part by applying the deficiency twice to the base: 1000 plus twice minus 4 is 1000 minus 8, which gives 992. Equivalently, reduce 996 by a further 4.
Build the right part by squaring the deficiency: minus 4 times minus 4 gives 16. Because the base 1000 has three zeros, this right part has to occupy a three-digit slot.

solution.operation: Pad the right part to 3 digit(s)
solution.description: Pad the right part to fill its slot. 16 is only two digits, so one leading zero is added to give 016. Skipping this pad would shift the digits and collapse the answer to 99216.
Set the two parts side by side, left first: 992 followed by the three-digit block 016 reads as 992016.
Check the shortcut against the algebraic identity for a squared difference: 1000 squared minus twice 1000 times 4 plus 4 squared also gives 992016.

common_mistakes: Writing the right part as 16 instead of the padded 016, which drops a place and gives 99216.
Applying the deficiency only once and taking 996 as the left part instead of subtracting a further 4 to reach 992.
